context.pr_body:
Benchmarks have just started failing, see #3972, so it seems like a good time to remove them.

See #3881, #1810, https://github.com/samuelcolvin/pydantic/issues/1939#issuecomment-695799667 #1425 and many other issues for an explanation of why I'm removing benchmarks.

TL;DR - they're wrong, they're a burden to maintain, they're controversial, they don't really belong in pydantic - they've outlived their usefulness.

In future it would be great if:
* we had a way of benchmarking pydantic between versions to improve performance and avoid performance slipping - I don't have time to do this now, I might in future
* it might also be cool if someone build a comparison of different data validation libraries, a bit like the [framework benchmarks](https://www.techempower.com/benchmarks/). But this would be a big piece of work and is way outside the bounds of pydantic

## Summary of changes

* internal logic has been move (mostly) into the `_internal` module - this is to provide a clear differentiating between the public API and internal functions
* Type constraints (like `constr`, `UUID5` `FilePath`) having been converted to type annotations, although some have an alias to simplicity

review_comments:
This `**extra` has been used to add stuff to JSON Schema.

But in some cases, people pass other stuff here expecting it to be used later or for other purposes, but then it also affects JSON Schema.

I would like to ask to make it a single keyword argument `extra` instead of `**extra`, or alternatively, to have another single argument `json_schema_extra` so that extensions for JSON Schema can be apart from extra values passed here for other purposes.

I haven't seen a use for this apart from JSON Schema, and the fact that it makes `Field()` accept any keyword arguments makes editors not complain about arguments that actually do nothing. I've seen this sometimes, e.g. recently with a `Field(required=True)`, but `required` is not a valid argument, if it's required or not is defined by the absence of a `default`. But the code seemed fine and linters passed, because it was taken by the catch all `**extra`.

It's a breaking change, but I think it's totally worth it and this is the right time for those changes.
This makes a lot of sense. It would also be easy to put through a deprecation cycle if necessary (just merging the dicts and emitting a warning if `**extra` is not empty)
Totally agree, done.
Amazing, thanks!

## Change Summary

Needs https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10313 first, as this relies on dataclasses respecting `defer_build`.

The idea is to focus on schema building during benchmarks and not the actual model definition. While for most cases this part represents a marginal percentage of the time, in some cases significant time is spent in other code paths. For example, the one with dataclasses being defined:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01b09f22-70d1-4f7a-bf51-66014afbe0ba)

Almost half the time is spent in the creation of stdlib dataclasses.

In another PR, I'll add benchmarks focusing on the model definition, specifically namespace stuff.

context.pr_title: Move core schema generation logic for path types inside the `GenerateSchema` class
context.pr_body:
Some (verbose) context: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/10036

I'm trying to remove the use of `prepare_pydantic_annotations_for_known_type` internally. We call this function in order to to pull metadata off of types and inject said metadata's constraints into core schema. This is bad practice, as we generally advertise being religious about respecting metadata order when building schema, but we violate that principle here.

Though these checks don't drag much on performance, they do significantly clutter our internal schema generation logic. They represent the old pattern (we have since deprecated) of supporting a `__pydantic_prepare_annotations__` method.

For example, we used to pull string constraint data like `min_length` off of a `Path` like annotation + apply that to the inner `core_schema.str_schema()` or `core_schema.bytes_schema()`.

This removes support for constraints like `max_length`, `min_length`, and `strip_whitespace` or other string constraints on `Path` types. Users should implement these constraints with custom validators. **This should be advertised in the v2.11 changelog.**
issue_titles: My take on suggested refactors for applying annotations
review_comments: As mentioned above, I'd really prefer if this wasn't the long term solution here.
It's notable that we add hacky support for `min_length` and `max_length` below, but we don't support things like `strip_whitespace` or `to_upper` - those are now broken for path like types.

Also I think people will mean "the number of characters" not "the number of bytes".

I'd love @PrettyWood @hramezani @tiangolo @adriangb and others to review this. Having to fix some suggestions, but given how big this is, I might defer some suggestions to subsequent PRs.

I'm sorry there's so much noise - obviously it would be great if the interesting bits could be in a different PR to the refactoring, but that wasn't possible while keeping tests "passing".

Test situation now:
* 1367 passed
* 92 skipped
* 732 xfailed - marked as allowed to fail to keep CI passing
* 210 xpassed - in files marked as allowed to fail, but passing

There's a lot still to do, but the core functionality is now working using pydantic-core.

## Summary of changes

* internal logic has been move (mostly) into the `_internal` module - this is to provide a clear differentiating between the public API and internal functions
* Type constraints (like `constr`, `UUID5` `FilePath`) having been converted to type annotations, although some have an alias to simplicity
* Most of the logic to generate pydantic-core schema from python types is done
* test modules that are mostly failing (or make no sense at the moment) have been marked as xfail, as features are fixed, we can remove the xfails and fix the tests
* mypy, pyright and linting are passing ~~(though the mypy tests are currently xfail), fixed~~
* docs examples are not run at the moment, re-building docs is probably the biggest thing to do
* model methods like `dict()` have not yet been renamed, we'll do that on a future PR

Before merging we need to decide on https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/307.

---

In terms of next steps, I'm going to create issues now rather than listing here.

context.pr_body:
fix #4666

**Things left to resolve:**

* [x] ~URLs~ Created an issue for this: #5095
	* [ ] Should minLength/maxLength be set on AnyUrl? (Class was moved from pydantic to pydantic_core)
	* [ ] Are we eliminating stricturl? Is the same functionality ported to pydantic_core in some manner?
		* What is the migration path?
	* **Tentative plan:** If it's possible to achieve the same functionality, drop stricturl and add notes to the migration guide

* [x] Json type
	* Is it okay to change Json[int]'s schema from {'type': 'number'} to {'type': 'string', 'format': 'json-string'}?
	* Change has been made

* [x] ~Callable type~ Created an issue for this: #5096 
	* How should we handle JSON schema generation for fields with type callable? (See, e.g., `tests.test_schema.test_callable_type`)
	* **Tentative plan:** Not sure.

* [x] ~Decimal~ Relevant issues: #1511 and #5072
	* What should the Decimal schema be?
	* **Tentative plan:** Need to come to a consensus; https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/1511 may be relevant
		* Note: although serialization and parsing are different, I think for FastAPI/OpenAPI purposes it is important that the JSON schema be compatible with the serialization type. (Or else generated clients will produce type errors if an API returns a Decimal.) Happy to discuss this more.

* [ ] `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__`
	* [x] Do we retain backwards compatibility with the name `__modify_schema__`, or force migration to `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__`?
		* **Plan:** Backwards compatible with `__modify_schema__`; new syntax in `__pydantic_json_schema__`
		* Do signature introspection for passing kwargs
	* [ ] Do we support any args/kwargs for `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__` besides the schema itself?
		* Do we pass any info to it from FieldInfo? The CoreSchema? A "source" object? (Could be useful when working with custom generics)
		* **Tentative plan:**
		    * Because this isn't overriding anything, we can just do signature introspection for different sets of arguments
		    * Need to decide how to handle this on enums and fields. I think it's a plain classmethod on enums with similar signature to what it is for models.

* [x] `'definitions'` -> `'$defs'`
    * [x] Should we change the key `'definitions'` to `'$defs'` everywhere? This is in line with JSON schema 2020-12, but it would be nice to confirm this won't break any important tooling (e.g., openapi-generator).
        * Change has been made (see `tests.test_schema.test_schema_with_refs`; openapi doesn't actually use the definitions key anyway, and FastAPI will change out the `$defs` key as appropriate.)

I'm pretty sure I added these functions in the first JSON Schema implementation to reuse them in FastAPI.

TL;DR: I vote to just remove them, at least for now.

If I remember correctly, I separated the logic in some of these functions in the way I expected to need it later in FastAPI, but before building FastAPI (not even the name was there). And in the end, I didn't really need all of them, and I actually needed others that I had to extract, copy or recreate. So, it was a bit of premature optimization/abstraction.

I think if anything around this needs to be done when integrating FastAPI, it's better in a future PR on top, building exactly what is really needed.

...and now I don't think there's any risk/fear that you would decide not to support features needed in Pydantic to integrate it with FastAPI properly. 😅

To be honest, I don't remember this `model_config`, I guess this is equivalent to the previous inner `class Config` but with better typing support, etc. right?

There are now new/better ways to update the JSON Schema with a method, right? If so, I would vote to remove it, reduce the options, and combinations of logic variables to consider, test, and learn (for users).

Also, if the decision was to keep it, it should be `json_schema_extra`, as in `Field()`, for consistency and to avoid confusion with the Pydantic Core Schema.

Yes, please! Remove that and let editors, linters, and Python error out. 😎

I mean, I don't take the decisions here... but yes, please! 🙏😅

I've seen quite some errors in the wild that can be reduced to Field() accepting any kwargs, people assuming they are valid, and even more, those things being reflected in JSON Schema, OpenAPI, Swagger UI... which adds another false confidence that "it's working".

E.g. with things like `required`, `nullable`.

I'm not fully sure because I never used it but I think this was equivalent to `Field(json_schema_extra=<blah blah>)`.

I would vote to remove it and only keep that in one place, the `Field()`, closer to the thing it is related to (each field).

> ...and now I don't think there's any risk/fear that you would decide not to support features needed in Pydantic to integrate it with FastAPI properly. 

😅

> To be honest, I don't remember this model_config, I guess this is equivalent to the previous inner class Config but with better typing support, etc. right?

Not sure if the typing support is better (😅), but yes, it is replacing the inner class Config.

There are new ways to update the schema, but I think they (at least as of the writing of this comment) involve a bit more ceremony than this (overriding methods, instantiating the JsonSchemaMisc type, etc.).

In general I think I'm in favor of reducing the amount of stuff in model_config where appropriate, and this seems like a good opportunity; I think the main change I'll make is changing the JsonSchemaMisc dataclass I have added to just be a TypedDict. While I liked having the methods, I think it will be fine to move them elsewhere and I think using a TypedDict will make it easier for users to pick up (and with less boilerplate).
I think we should just support `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__` (or whatever it end su being called) on a model, then anything else should only be supported for backwards compatibility.

def resolve_condecimal(cls):  # type: ignore[no-untyped-def]
    min_value = cls.ge
    max_value = cls.le
    if cls.gt is not None:
        assert min_value is None, 'Set `gt` or `ge`, but not both'
        min_value = cls.gt
    if cls.lt is not None:
        assert max_value is None, 'Set `lt` or `le`, but not both'
        max_value = cls.lt
    s = st.decimals(min_value, max_value, allow_nan=False, places=cls.decimal_places)
    if cls.lt is not None:
        s = s.filter(lambda d: d < cls.lt)
    if cls.gt is not None:
        s = s.filter(lambda d: cls.gt < d)
    return s

context.commit_message:
Allow applying serializers and constraints to named/ref schemas (#6007)

Co-authored-by: Terrence Dorsey <terrend@mishu.com>
context.pr_title: Allow applying serializers and constraints to named/ref schemas
context.pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/5998

This makes some fundamental changes to core schema and json schema building.
In particular:
- Any schemas with a `"ref"` or `"$ref"` we immediately stick into `"definitions"` or `"$defs"` respectively. I added a `resolve_ref_schema` method to `GetCoreSchemaHandler` that is analogous to the one we already had in `GetJsonSchemaHandler`. This means that implementing `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` can be more complex because you're forced to deal with refs explicitly, but it resolves several inconsistencies and bugs.
- I was able to make automatic unpacking of `"ref"` schemas work for the source type itself, which means that if you implement `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` on `Model(BaseModel)` and call `handler(source_type)` you don't get back a `"ref"` schema, we unpack it for you because a source type should edit its own schema in-place.
- We no longer "automatically unpack" `"$ref"` JSON schemas. To avoid making JSON schema generation more difficult we were previously automatically unpacking `"$ref"` for every handler call, but this was complex and led to inconsistencies the same as mentioned above. This leads to regression for the case of "source types" because as per above those should have the `"ref"` unpacked for them. Fixing this will require some more work that I would like to defer from this PR. In particular, when we generate the JSON schema now we just have a list of functions to call, we have no way of knowing if they came from metadata in `Annotated` or `__get_pydantic_json_schema__` on the source type itself.


Selected Reviewer: @dmontagu

In #5052 we validated it by creating a ton of generics and measuring memory usage, not by checking the size of the cache. I'm a bit surprised by your tests behavior but not _too_ surprised, I don't know if it's easy to measure these things at this fine of a level.

I did a sanity check:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete

del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

assert len(cache) == 0  # actually 1
```

So it seems this would not work in the first place!

Ok I think I found the issue:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]
cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete
del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

referrer = next(iter(gc.get_referrers(next(cache.values()))))
print(referrer)  # <functools._lru_cache_wrapper object at 0x102dee560>
print(referrer.__module__)  # typing
```

So it looks like this cache inside of `_tp_cache` of `typing.py` may be holding onto a reference.
It has a `maxsize` of 128, which basically means that the `WeakValueDict` will act as a regular dict for the _last_ 128 things that got run through it!

That explains why the test that creates thousands of objects and measures memory consumption looks like it's not accumulating but this one measuring just 1 reference does.

from weakref import WeakValueDictionary
from pydantic import BaseModel

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(BaseModel, Generic[T]):

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

def create_and_del() -> None:

    cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete
    del Concrete

create_and_del()
gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

for r in gc.get_referrers(next(cache.values())):
    print(r, end="\n\n")
```

I can confirm the memory leak issue is solved and the memray test is passing for me locally; not sure exactly how this should be modified for compatibility with v2.

If you find this crazy _early and _late cache key business hard to understand, I can explain in more detail (probably makes sense to add comments to these functions but wanted to see if you ended up wanting to simplify it first).

This approach was necessary to get `Model[List[T]][int]` to be the same type as `Model[List[int]]`. It could be modified to not use two different cache keys at different points, but the `_early_cache_key` is optimized to be as quick to compute as possible (for repeated-access speed), and the `_late_cache_key` is optimized to be as "correct" as possible, so that two types that are ultimately the same after resolving the type arguments will always produce cache hits.

If we only wanted one (or two in the case of single-item-inputs to `__class_getitem__`) cache keys per type, we would either need to always use the slower/more computationally intensive logic associated with `_late_cache_key`, or would need to accept that `Model[List[T]][int]` is a different type than `Model[List[T]][int]`. I'm hesitant to accept this last point given that currently, an instance of type `Model[List[T]][int]` will fail validation for a field of type `Model[List[int]]`. Refactor and optimize schema cleaning logic (#11244)

The existing `_WalkCoreSchema` logic is replaced by a new schema cleaning logic. While the existing logic was traversing the core schemas multiple times to:
- collect schemas with references (replacing them with `'definition-reference'` schemas)
- counting the number of definition references
- replace `'definition-reference'` by its definition, if possible
- figure out schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied
- collect invalid schemas

We know apply a single *read-only* pass on the core schemas to:
- collect all definition references, so that we can drop unused definitions
- collect `'definition-reference'` if it appears only once, and then mutate it *in place* to be the definition it points to.
- collect schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied

The two biggest changes here are:
- the schema traversing is read-only, there's not initial copy of it like we used to do in the first `_WalkCoreSchema` pass. Because we mutate `'definition-reference'` schemas in place, this could lead to other model schemas mutated. In practice, this shouldn't happen.
- Referenceable schemas are not transformed into `'definition-reference'` schemas first. If a schema is fetched from a `__pydantic_core_schema__` property, and this schema contains a referenceable schema that is also present in the root schema, they won't be collected as a single definition.

The extra step to collect invalid schemas was also removed, although this could be added back without any performance degradation.

The schema traversing code is implemented in Python. Doing so in Rust provides a small performance improvement, but having it defined in Python provides easier maintenance. This might get revisited in the future.

Thanks @MarkusSintonen for looking into this first and designing the new schema traversing logic.

Co-authored-by: Markus Sintonen <markus.sintonen@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: sydney-runkle <sydneymarierunkle@gmail.com>

## Change Summary

Closes https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, fixes #10285 

This is slightly identical to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, with the difference that:
- only contains the relevant changes (the rest was split off in smaller PRs)
- Implements the schema traversing logic in Python instead of in `pydantic-core`. Out of 3-4s, the rust implementation takes 20ms, while the Python one takes 230ms. I don't know yet if we should keep it in Python (it has advantages: type checking, easier debugging).
- simplifies the schema traversing logic (simplified context class, etc)
- simplifies schema inlining logic (no need to check for recursive refs)

Concerns (1 so far):

- Consequence of the new schema traversing logic: we don't traverse schemas that have been unpacked from another model. With the following:
  ```python
  from pydantic import BaseModel

  class StandaloneModel(BaseModel): ...

  class M1(BaseModel):
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  The core schema of M1 is:

  <details>
  <summary>M1 core schema</summary>  

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'model',
  │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970984129568',
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   }
  │   │   },
  │   │   'model_name': 'M1',
  │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   },
  │   'config': {'title': 'M1'},
  │   'ref': '__main__.M1:94970983986336',
  │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  }
  ```
  </details>

  As you can see, `Model` is inlined inside the core schema for field `m`.

  Now if you do:

  ```python
  class M2(BaseModel):
      m1: M1
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  `StandaloneModel` is used twice in `M2` (in `m` and `M1.m`). However, the inlined core schema for `M1.StandaloneModel` is not transformed back into a `'definition-ref'` schema (and doing so would require a copy of the schema to avoid mutating the core schema of `M1` from `M2`!):

  <details>
  <summary>M2 core schema</summary>  

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'model',
  │   'cls': <class '__main__.M2'>,
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   'm1': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970985756064',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   }
  │   │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'model_name': 'M1',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'M1'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.M1:94970985783632',
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970985756064',
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   }
  │   │   },
  │   │   'model_name': 'M2',
  │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   },
  │   'config': {'title': 'M2'},
  │   'ref': '__main__.M2:94970985797664',
  │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  }
  ```
  </details>

  On `main`, `StandaloneModel` is properly stored in definitions, and `'definition-ref'` schemas are used:

  <details>
  <summary>M2 core schema on main</summary>

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'definitions',
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.M2'>,
  │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   │   'm1': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'schema_ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:101823146688192'},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   }
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'model_name': 'M1',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'M1'},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.M1:101823149646624',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'definition-ref', 'schema_ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:101823146688192'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   │   }
  │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   'model_name': 'M2',
  │   │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   │   },
  │   │   'config': {'title': 'M2'},
  │   │   'ref': '__main__.M2:101823148327728',
  │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   },
  │   'definitions': [
  │   │   {
  │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:101823146688192',
  │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   }
  │   ]
  }
  ```
  </details>

  Both approaches are valid, but it might be that this cause unexpected issues (JSON Schema differences, etc). Regarding memory consumption, it is slightly affected. Taking the [`k8s_v2.py`](https://gist.github.com/Viicos/bd9b3b0e3fbee62838626b07b311f3af) file as an example (it is a good one because the "issue" described here happens several times in it), we don't see any increase/decrease in %RAM consumption, although profile over time differs:

context.pr_body:
This reverts #4224.

fix #4458, fix #4468. Replaces #4469 and #4461.

There are a number of problems with #4224:
1. It re-encodes existing percent encoded URLs, this was reported in #4458 and could be fixed by #4469
2. It wrongly encoded `/`, this could also be fixed by #4469
3. It wrongly encoded `+`, this was reported in #4468 and could also be fixed by #4469
4. It would require us to rebuild virtually all URLs, currently we only rebuild URLs with "international" domains, if I enable `rebuild` for all URL validation, lots of tests fail, fixing those tests involves significant changes and we're well into the "this is not really suitable for a patch release" territory.

Therefore after some consideration and discussion with other pydantic maintainers (and with a heavy heart), I've decided the best approach is to remove percentage encoding from URL logic until V2.

Long term (e.g. in V2) I think we should use an external library (either in python or rust) to perform URL parsing and validation.

This is the big one :scream:.

I'd love @PrettyWood @hramezani @tiangolo @adriangb and others to review this. Having to fix some suggestions, but given how big this is, I might defer some suggestions to subsequent PRs.

I'm sorry there's so much noise - obviously it would be great if the interesting bits could be in a different PR to the refactoring, but that wasn't possible while keeping tests "passing".

Test situation now:
* 1367 passed
* 92 skipped
* 732 xfailed - marked as allowed to fail to keep CI passing
* 210 xpassed - in files marked as allowed to fail, but passing

There's a lot still to do, but the core functionality is now working using pydantic-core.

## Summary of changes

* internal logic has been move (mostly) into the `_internal` module - this is to provide a clear differentiating between the public API and internal functions
* Type constraints (like `constr`, `UUID5` `FilePath`) having been converted to type annotations, although some have an alias to simplicity
* Most of the logic to generate pydantic-core schema from python types is done
* test modules that are mostly failing (or make no sense at the moment) have been marked as xfail, as features are fixed, we can remove the xfails and fix the tests
* mypy, pyright and linting are passing ~~(though the mypy tests are currently xfail), fixed~~
* docs examples are not run at the moment, re-building docs is probably the biggest thing to do
* model methods like `dict()` have not yet been renamed, we'll do that on a future PR

Before merging we need to decide on https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/307.

---

In terms of next steps, I'm going to create issues now rather than listing here.

context.commit_message:
Refactor and optimize schema cleaning logic (#11244)

The existing `_WalkCoreSchema` logic is replaced by a new schema cleaning logic. While the existing logic was traversing the core schemas multiple times to:
- collect schemas with references (replacing them with `'definition-reference'` schemas)
- counting the number of definition references
- replace `'definition-reference'` by its definition, if possible
- figure out schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied
- collect invalid schemas

We know apply a single *read-only* pass on the core schemas to:
- collect all definition references, so that we can drop unused definitions
- collect `'definition-reference'` if it appears only once, and then mutate it *in place* to be the definition it points to.
- collect schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied

The two biggest changes here are:
- the schema traversing is read-only, there's not initial copy of it like we used to do in the first `_WalkCoreSchema` pass. Because we mutate `'definition-reference'` schemas in place, this could lead to other model schemas mutated. In practice, this shouldn't happen.
- Referenceable schemas are not transformed into `'definition-reference'` schemas first. If a schema is fetched from a `__pydantic_core_schema__` property, and this schema contains a referenceable schema that is also present in the root schema, they won't be collected as a single definition.

The extra step to collect invalid schemas was also removed, although this could be added back without any performance degradation.

The schema traversing code is implemented in Python. Doing so in Rust provides a small performance improvement, but having it defined in Python provides easier maintenance. This might get revisited in the future.

Thanks @MarkusSintonen for looking into this first and designing the new schema traversing logic.

Co-authored-by: Markus Sintonen <markus.sintonen@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: sydney-runkle <sydneymarierunkle@gmail.com>

## Change Summary

Closes https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, fixes #10285 

This is slightly identical to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, with the difference that:
- only contains the relevant changes (the rest was split off in smaller PRs)
- Implements the schema traversing logic in Python instead of in `pydantic-core`. Out of 3-4s, the rust implementation takes 20ms, while the Python one takes 230ms. I don't know yet if we should keep it in Python (it has advantages: type checking, easier debugging).
- simplifies the schema traversing logic (simplified context class, etc)
- simplifies schema inlining logic (no need to check for recursive refs)

Concerns (1 so far):

- Consequence of the new schema traversing logic: we don't traverse schemas that have been unpacked from another model. With the following:
  ```python
  from pydantic import BaseModel

  class StandaloneModel(BaseModel): ...

  class M1(BaseModel):
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  The core schema of M1 is:

  <details>
  <summary>M1 core schema</summary>  

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'model',
  │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970984129568',
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   }
  │   │   },
  │   │   'model_name': 'M1',
  │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   },
  │   'config': {'title': 'M1'},
  │   'ref': '__main__.M1:94970983986336',
  │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  }
  ```
  </details>

  As you can see, `Model` is inlined inside the core schema for field `m`.

  Now if you do:

  ```python
  class M2(BaseModel):
      m1: M1
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970985756064',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}

Follow up to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10846

See the description of that PR for more detail.

One consequence here is slightly different behavior for `maxlen` being set for `deque` types, but I think this is worth the significant simplification in internal logic we see here.

`max_length` constraints are still enforced, but we no longer monkeypatch the `maxlen` from `max_length` on the deque. If users want this, they should write a custom validator.

I'll be writing an in depth explanation of changes in the changelog for v2.11 related to this PR sequence.

Found another edge case, related to `Callable`. It turns out tat that the "input arguments" part of the type is a list of types, which means that `resolve_type_hints` fails. Here's a test case:

```py
@skip_36
def test_generic_with_callable():
    T = TypeVar('T')
    U = TypeVar('U')

    class VeryInnerModel(GenericModel, Generic[T, U]):
        t: T
        u: U
        some_callable: Callable[[Optional[int], str], None]

    VeryInnerModel[str, U]
```

This results in the following failure: `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` when `[Optional[int], str]` is used as a key in the `typevars_map`

Turns out there are a number of problems with `Callable`:
1. Need to handle it in `resolve_type_hint` properly
2. Need to handle it in `_has_typevar` properly

```suggestion
        return type_[tuple(resolve_type_hint(t, typevars_map) for t in type_.__parameters__)]
    if isinstance(type_, list):
        return [resolve_type_hints(element, typevars_map) for element in type_]        
```

```suggestion
            parameters = tuple({v: None for v in typevars_map.values() if isinstance(v, TypeVar)})
```

Unfortunately `lenient_issubclass` fails if `field_type` is a generic alias.

```python

```
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/dek/Documents/Code/pydantic/pydantic/utils.py", line 145, in lenient_issubclass
    return isinstance(cls, type) and issubclass(cls, class_or_tuple)
  File "/home/dek/anaconda/envs/pydantic-39/lib/python3.9/abc.py", line 102, in __subclasscheck__
    return _abc_subclasscheck(cls, subclass)
TypeError: issubclass() arg 1 must be a class
```

The exact logic is that:
```
isinstance(list[int], type)
```
returns `True` but then `issubclass` needs a `class` which `list[int]` is not.

I can add workaround code to lenient_issubclass but I wasn't sure that would be the right thing to do given how many places lenient_issubclass is used and this sort of handling of typehints seemed relatively specialized towards generics.
I moved this to a more generic "all_identical" function (moved that to utils) and added some docs/examples/tests.  Hope it's clearer now.

I looked through `pydantic.typing` again and there's nothing in there that does this.  

The code is quite geared towards the `generics` module (i.e. I don't see anywhere else in pydantic where this would be used), but the code itself is relatively generic in the sense that it just recursively replaces types according to a a map/dictionary.

It does have to reference the `GenericModel` though so I think I would keep it in there until there is somewhere else that needs this sort of recursive type map.

I also though there may have been confusion regarding the `resolve_annotations` in the `pydantic.typing` module, so I renamed this to `replace_types` since that's what it does (not really specific to type hints)

Better?  There's also a test specific to this function.  If you'd like I can add an example in the docstring, I'm unsure about the policy of docstring examples vs. tests (I don't think doctests are being run in ci if I'm not mistaken)
I used `pydantic.typing.display_as_type` and added a case to that instead, which cleans this whole function up quite a lot.  Hope it's clearer now.
See below, got rid of the weird stuff with `pydantic.typing.display_as_type`

        assert CheckModel(**kwargs).model_dump()[field] == result

context.pr_body:
fix #4666

**Things left to resolve:**

* [x] ~URLs~ Created an issue for this: #5095
	* [ ] Should minLength/maxLength be set on AnyUrl? (Class was moved from pydantic to pydantic_core)
	* [ ] Are we eliminating stricturl? Is the same functionality ported to pydantic_core in some manner?
		* What is the migration path?
	* **Tentative plan:** If it's possible to achieve the same functionality, drop stricturl and add notes to the migration guide

* [x] Json type
	* Is it okay to change Json[int]'s schema from {'type': 'number'} to {'type': 'string', 'format': 'json-string'}?
	* Change has been made

* [x] ~Callable type~ Created an issue for this: #5096 
	* How should we handle JSON schema generation for fields with type callable? (See, e.g., `tests.test_schema.test_callable_type`)
	* **Tentative plan:** Not sure.

* [x] ~Decimal~ Relevant issues: #1511 and #5072
	* What should the Decimal schema be?
	* **Tentative plan:** Need to come to a consensus; https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/issues/1511 may be relevant
		* Note: although serialization and parsing are different, I think for FastAPI/OpenAPI purposes it is important that the JSON schema be compatible with the serialization type. (Or else generated clients will produce type errors if an API returns a Decimal.) Happy to discuss this more.

* [ ] `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__`
	* [x] Do we retain backwards compatibility with the name `__modify_schema__`, or force migration to `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__`?
		* **Plan:** Backwards compatible with `__modify_schema__`; new syntax in `__pydantic_json_schema__`
		* Do signature introspection for passing kwargs
	* [ ] Do we support any args/kwargs for `__pydantic_modify_json_schema__` besides the schema itself?
		* Do we pass any info to it from FieldInfo? The CoreSchema? A "source" object? (Could be useful when working with custom generics)
		* **Tentative plan:**
		    * Because this isn't overriding anything, we can just do signature introspection for different sets of arguments
		    * Need to decide how to handle this on enums and fields. I think it's a plain classmethod on enums with similar signature to what it is for models.

* [x] `'definitions'` -> `'$defs'`
    * [x] Should we change the key `'definitions'` to `'$defs'` everywhere? This is in line with JSON schema 2020-12, but it would be nice to confirm this won't break any important tooling (e.g., openapi-generator).
        * Change has been made (see `tests.test_schema.test_schema_with_refs`; openapi doesn't actually use the definitions key anyway, and FastAPI will change out the `$defs` key as appropriate.)

## Change Summary

- Refactor the `_typing_extra` module to:
  - make use of https://typing-extensions.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#runtime-use-of-types. In a lot of places, we are only checking for `some_obj is typing(_extensions).SomeType` which can break at any time if `typing_extensions` backports some changes from Python, in which case `typing.SomeType is not typing_extensions.SomeType`.
  - Cleanup/simplify some `is_*` functions (e.g. `is_newtype`, `is_classvar`).
  - Add a new `is_classvar_annotation` function, that should be used in most cases. This function handles `ClassVar` being wrapped in `Annotated`, and also stringified annotations.
  - Rename `all_literal_values` to `literal_values`, replacing the unused `literal_values` function. When we drop support for Python 3.8, replace usage with a plain `get_args`.
  - Remove unecessary `is_dataclass` function, `dataclasses.is_dataclass` provides a type guard return annotation.
- Adapt the codebase to use the new constructs. In some cases, this does fix some actual bugs

context.commit_message:
Refactor and optimize schema cleaning logic (#11244)

The existing `_WalkCoreSchema` logic is replaced by a new schema cleaning logic. While the existing logic was traversing the core schemas multiple times to:
- collect schemas with references (replacing them with `'definition-reference'` schemas)
- counting the number of definition references
- replace `'definition-reference'` by its definition, if possible
- figure out schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied
- collect invalid schemas

We know apply a single *read-only* pass on the core schemas to:
- collect all definition references, so that we can drop unused definitions
- collect `'definition-reference'` if it appears only once, and then mutate it *in place* to be the definition it points to.
- collect schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied

The two biggest changes here are:
- the schema traversing is read-only, there's not initial copy of it like we used to do in the first `_WalkCoreSchema` pass. Because we mutate `'definition-reference'` schemas in place, this could lead to other model schemas mutated. In practice, this shouldn't happen.
- Referenceable schemas are not transformed into `'definition-reference'` schemas first. If a schema is fetched from a `__pydantic_core_schema__` property, and this schema contains a referenceable schema that is also present in the root schema, they won't be collected as a single definition.

The extra step to collect invalid schemas was also removed, although this could be added back without any performance degradation.

The schema traversing code is implemented in Python. Doing so in Rust provides a small performance improvement, but having it defined in Python provides easier maintenance. This might get revisited in the future.

Thanks @MarkusSintonen for looking into this first and designing the new schema traversing logic.

Co-authored-by: Markus Sintonen <markus.sintonen@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: sydney-runkle <sydneymarierunkle@gmail.com>
context.pr_title: Refactor and optimize schema cleaning logic
context.pr_body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! -->
<!-- Unless your change is trivial, please create an issue to discuss the change before creating a PR -->

## Change Summary

Closes https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, fixes #10285 

This is slightly identical to https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/pull/10655, with the difference that:
- only contains the relevant changes (the rest was split off in smaller PRs)
- Implements the schema traversing logic in Python instead of in `pydantic-core`. Out of 3-4s, the rust implementation takes 20ms, while the Python one takes 230ms. I don't know yet if we should keep it in Python (it has advantages: type checking, easier debugging).
- simplifies the schema traversing logic (simplified context class, etc)
- simplifies schema inlining logic (no need to check for recursive refs)

Concerns (1 so far):

- Consequence of the new schema traversing logic: we don't traverse schemas that have been unpacked from another model. With the following:
  ```python
  from pydantic import BaseModel

  class StandaloneModel(BaseModel): ...

  class M1(BaseModel):
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  The core schema of M1 is:

  <details>
  <summary>M1 core schema</summary>  

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'model',
  │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970984129568',
  │   │   │   │   │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  │   │   │   │   },
  │   │   │   │   'metadata': {}
  │   │   │   }
  │   │   },
  │   │   'model_name': 'M1',
  │   │   'computed_fields': []
  │   },
  │   'config': {'title': 'M1'},
  │   'ref': '__main__.M1:94970983986336',
  │   'metadata': {'<stripped>'}
  }
  ```
  </details>

  As you can see, `Model` is inlined inside the core schema for field `m`.

  Now if you do:

  ```python
  class M2(BaseModel):
      m1: M1
      m: StandaloneModel
  ```

  `StandaloneModel` is used twice in `M2` (in `m` and `M1.m`). However, the inlined core schema for `M1.StandaloneModel` is not transformed back into a `'definition-ref'` schema (and doing so would require a copy of the schema to avoid mutating the core schema of `M1` from `M2`!):

  <details>
  <summary>M2 core schema</summary>  

  ```python
  {
  │   'type': 'model',
  │   'cls': <class '__main__.M2'>,
  │   'schema': {
  │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   'm1': {
  │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.M1'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-fields',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   'fields': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'm': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model-field',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'type': 'model',
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'cls': <class '__main__.StandaloneModel'>,
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'schema': {'type': 'model-fields', 'fields': {}, 'model_name': 'StandaloneModel', 'computed_fields': []},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'config': {'title': 'StandaloneModel'},
  │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   │   'ref': '__main__.StandaloneModel:94970985756064',

issue_titles: [Bug] Experimental pipeline .len() adds redundant Python-level validation for native length types
review_comments:
🟠 **High** `experimental/pipeline.py:496` Chained ordering constraints overwrite each other instead of being composed, so `validate_as(datetime.date).gt(date(2025, 1, 1)).gt(date(2020, 1, 1))` retains only the latter `gt` constraint and accepts dates from 2021 through 2025. The native-schema fast path should preserve both constraints, for example by falling back to validator composition when the schema already has the same constraint.
🚀 Reply "fix it for me" or copy this AI Prompt for your agent: ```text In file @pydantic/experimental/pipeline.py around line 496: Chained ordering constraints overwrite each other instead of being composed, so `validate_as(datetime.date).gt(date(2025, 1, 1)).gt(date(2020, 1, 1))` retains only the latter `gt` constraint and accepts dates from 2021 through 2025. The native-schema fast path should preserve both constraints, for example by falling back to validator composition when the schema already has the same constraint. ```

**Low: Earlier pipeline constraints are overwritten**

Because the schema remains a native type, a later `len()` call replaces its existing `min_length` or `max_length`; for example, `.len(10, 20).len(1, 30)` now accepts a two-character string even though both pipeline steps should apply. The same regression affects repeated ordering constraints on the newly added native types. Preserve the stricter existing bound or retain an after-validator when a corresponding constraint is already present.

When the `Len` constraint falls back to the Python-level `check_len`, the predicate string is always formatted as `length >= {min_len} and length <= {max_len}`. If `max_len is None`, this produces error messages like `Expected length >= 2 and length <= None`, which is confusing and user-facing. Also, `len(v)` is computed twice when `max_len` is set.

def validator(
    *fields: str,
    pre: bool = False,
    each_item: bool = False,
    always: bool = False,
    check_fields: bool = True,
    whole: bool = None,
    allow_reuse: bool = False,
) -> Callable[[AnyCallable], 'AnyClassMethod']:
    """
    Decorate methods on the class indicating that they should be used to validate fields
    :param fields: which field(s) the method should be called on
    :param pre: whether or not this validator should be called before the standard validators (else after)
    :param each_item: for complex objects (sets, lists etc.) whether to validate individual elements rather than the
      whole object
    :param always: whether this method and other validators should be called even if the value is missing
    :param check_fields: whether to check that the fields actually exist on the model
    :param allow_reuse: whether to track and raise an error if another validator refers to the decorated function
    """
    if not fields:
        raise ConfigError('validator with no fields specified')
    elif isinstance(fields[0], FunctionType):
        raise ConfigError(
            "validators should be used with fields and keyword arguments, not bare. "  # noqa: Q000
            "E.g. usage should be `@validator('<field_name>', ...)`"
        )
    elif not all(isinstance(field, str) for field in fields):
        raise ConfigError(
            "validator fields should be passed as separate string args. "  # noqa: Q000
            "E.g. usage should be `@validator('<field_name_1>', '<field_name_2>', ...)`"
        )

    if whole is not None:
        warnings.warn(
            'The "whole" keyword argument is deprecated, use "each_item" (inverse meaning, default False) instead',
            DeprecationWarning,
        )
        assert each_item is False, '"each_item" and "whole" conflict, remove "whole"'
        each_item = not whole

    def dec(f: AnyCallable) -> 'AnyClassMethod':
        f_cls = _prepare_validator(f, allow_reuse)
        setattr(
            f_cls,
            VALIDATOR_CONFIG_KEY,
            (
                fields,
                Validator(func=f_cls.__func__, pre=pre, each_item=each_item, always=always, check_fields=check_fields),
            ),
        )
        return f_cls

    return dec

@classmethod
    def _build_url(cls, m: Match[str], url: str, parts: 'Parts') -> 'MultiHostDsn':
        hosts_parts: list[HostParts] = []
        host_re = host_regex()
        for host in m.groupdict()['hosts'].split(','):
            d: Parts = host_re.match(host).groupdict()  # type: ignore
            host, tld, host_type, rebuild = cls.validate_host(d)
            port = d.get('port')
            cls._validate_port(port)
            hosts_parts.append(
                {
                    'host': host,
                    'host_type': host_type,
                    'tld': tld,
                    'rebuild': rebuild,
                    'port': port,
                }
            )

        if len(hosts_parts) > 1:
            return cls(
                None if any([hp['rebuild'] for hp in hosts_parts]) else url,
                scheme=parts['scheme'],
                user=parts['user'],
                password=parts['password'],
                path=parts['path'],
                query=parts['query'],
                fragment=parts['fragment'],
                host_type=None,
                hosts=hosts_parts,
            )
        else:
            # backwards compatibility with single host
            host_part = hosts_parts[0]
            return cls(
                None if host_part['rebuild'] else url,
                scheme=parts['scheme'],
                user=parts['user'],
                password=parts['password'],
                host=host_part['host'],
                tld=host_part['tld'],
                host_type=host_part['host_type'],
                port=host_part.get('port'),
                path=parts['path'],
                query=parts['query'],
                fragment=parts['fragment'],
            )

I'd love @PrettyWood @hramezani @tiangolo @adriangb and others to review this. Having to fix some suggestions, but given how big this is, I might defer some suggestions to subsequent PRs.

I'm sorry there's so much noise - obviously it would be great if the interesting bits could be in a different PR to the refactoring, but that wasn't possible while keeping tests "passing".

Test situation now:
* 1367 passed
* 92 skipped
* 732 xfailed - marked as allowed to fail to keep CI passing
* 210 xpassed - in files marked as allowed to fail, but passing

There's a lot still to do, but the core functionality is now working using pydantic-core.

## Summary of changes

* internal logic has been move (mostly) into the `_internal` module - this is to provide a clear differentiating between the public API and internal functions
* Type constraints (like `constr`, `UUID5` `FilePath`) having been converted to type annotations, although some have an alias to simplicity
* Most of the logic to generate pydantic-core schema from python types is done
* test modules that are mostly failing (or make no sense at the moment) have been marked as xfail, as features are fixed, we can remove the xfails and fix the tests
* mypy, pyright and linting are passing ~~(though the mypy tests are currently xfail), fixed~~
* docs examples are not run at the moment, re-building docs is probably the biggest thing to do
* model methods like `dict()` have not yet been renamed, we'll do that on a future PR

Before merging we need to decide on https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/307.

---

In terms of next steps, I'm going to create issues now rather than listing here.

Hi!

This is my first try to improve errors format (discussion can be found in #162). I'd like to get review on changes and discuss some points.

At first here are simple example which will be used to show new errors format:

```py
from typing import Dict, List, Union
from uuid import UUID

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class TestDict(BaseModel):
    x: int
    y: int
    z: str


class TestModel(BaseModel):
    a: List[TestDict]
    b: int
    c: TestDict
    d: Union[int, UUID]
    e: Dict[int, int]
    f: List[Union[int, UUID]]


try:
    TestModel.parse_obj({
        'a': [
            {
                'x': 'not_int',
                'y': 42,
                'z': 'string',
            },
        ],
        'b': 'string',
        'c': {
            'y': 42,
        },
        'd': 'string',
        'e': {
            'foo': 'bar',
        },
        'f': [
            'string',
        ],
    })
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.json())
```

And errors output:
```py
[
  {
    "loc": "a.0.x",
    "msg": "invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not_int'",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "b",
    "msg": "invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'string'",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "c.x",
    "msg": "field required",
    "type": "value_error.missing"
  },
  {
    "loc": "c.z",
    "msg": "field required",
    "type": "value_error.missing"
  },
  {
    "loc": "d",
    "msg": "invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'string'",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "d",
    "msg": "badly formed hexadecimal UUID string",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "e.key",
    "msg": "invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'foo'",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "f.0",
    "msg": "invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'string'",
    "type": "value_error"
  },
  {
    "loc": "f.0",
    "msg": "badly formed hexadecimal UUID string",
    "type": "value_error"
  }
]
```

Questions:
1. Is this format good to go (`msg` kept for backward compatibility and can be removed, `context` can be easily added)?
2. As you can see we are using `key` postfix if error occurred in dictionary key, is it okay?
3. As you can see there are two errors for field `d` (and `f.0`) because they are complex and contains sub fields, I think we need to expose this information in `loc`, maybe by using postfix, something like `d.sub.0` and `d.sub.1`. Any ideas?
4. Big question how to display errors in plain text? For now it's very simple:
```
a.0.x
  invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not_int' (type=value_error)
b
  invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'string' (type=value_error)
c.x
  field required (type=value_error.missing)
c.z
  field required (type=value_error.missing)
d

f.0
  invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'string' (type=value_error)
f.0
  badly formed hexadecimal UUID string (type=value_error)
```

def my_validator_function(
        tz_constraint: Union[str, None],
        value: dt.datetime,
        handler: Callable,
    ):
        """validate tz_constraint and tz_info"""

        # handle naive datetimes
        if tz_constraint is None:
            assert value.tzinfo is None
            return handler(value)

        # validate tz_constraint and tz-aware tzinfo
        assert tz_constraint in pytz.all_timezones
        result = handler(value)
        assert tz_constraint == str(result.tzinfo)

        return result

def _prepare_model_fields(
    created_model: Type[GenericModel],
    fields: Mapping[str, Any],
    instance_type_hints: Mapping[str, type],
    typevars_map: Mapping[Any, type],
) -> None:
    """
    Replace DeferredType fields with concrete type hints and prepare them.
    """

    for key, field in created_model.model_fields.items():
        if key not in fields:
            assert field.annotation.__class__ is not DeferredType
            # https://github.com/nedbat/coveragepy/issues/198
            continue  # pragma: no cover

        assert field.annotation.__class__ is DeferredType, field.annotation.__class__

        field_type_hint = instance_type_hints[key]
        concrete_type = replace_types(field_type_hint, typevars_map)
        field.annotation = concrete_type
        created_model.__annotations__[key] = concrete_type

In #5052 we validated it by creating a ton of generics and measuring memory usage, not by checking the size of the cache. I'm a bit surprised by your tests behavior but not _too_ surprised, I don't know if it's easy to measure these things at this fine of a level.

I did a sanity check:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete

del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

assert len(cache) == 0  # actually 1
```

So it seems this would not work in the first place!

Ok I think I found the issue:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]
cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete
del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

referrer = next(iter(gc.get_referrers(next(cache.values()))))
print(referrer)  # <functools._lru_cache_wrapper object at 0x102dee560>
print(referrer.__module__)  # typing
```

So it looks like this cache inside of `_tp_cache` of `typing.py` may be holding onto a reference.
It has a `maxsize` of 128, which basically means that the `WeakValueDict` will act as a regular dict for the _last_ 128 things that got run through it!

That explains why the test that creates thousands of objects and measures memory consumption looks like it's not accumulating but this one measuring just 1 reference does.

If you find this crazy _early and _late cache key business hard to understand, I can explain in more detail (probably makes sense to add comments to these functions but wanted to see if you ended up wanting to simplify it first).

This approach was necessary to get `Model[List[T]][int]` to be the same type as `Model[List[int]]`. It could be modified to not use two different cache keys at different points, but the `_early_cache_key` is optimized to be as quick to compute as possible (for repeated-access speed), and the `_late_cache_key` is optimized to be as "correct" as possible, so that two types that are ultimately the same after resolving the type arguments will always produce cache hits.

If we only wanted one (or two in the case of single-item-inputs to `__class_getitem__`) cache keys per type, we would either need to always use the slower/more computationally intensive logic associated with `_late_cache_key`, or would need to accept that `Model[List[T]][int]` is a different type than `Model[List[T]][int]`. I'm hesitant to accept this last point given that currently, an instance of type `Model[List[T]][int]` will fail validation for a field of type `Model[List[int]]`. That said, I think we may need to change that behavior anyway.

I did some digging into what was going on with the calls to get_args in the v1 cache key logic, and as far as I could tell the only thing it was really doing for us was helping us differentiate between the ordering of items in Unions (e.g., `Union[int, float]` vs. `Union[float, int]`). context.pr_body:
## Change Summary

Consistent `__repr__` and `__str__` method for all models, in general:
* `__str__` returns a human readable string representing the data the instances holds. Defined as something like "what you might show to an end user if you were lazy"
* `__repr__` is roughly `f'ClassName({str(self)})'`, except commas are used in separators to make 
 `eval(repr(m))` roughly equal to m

other changes:
* `__pretty__` method added to integrate with [python-devtools](https://python-devtools.helpmanual.io/)
* `display()` method on `SecretStr` and `SecretBytes` has been depreciated in favour of `str(s)
* (virtually unused and undocumented) `to_string()` method on `BaseModel` has been depreciated in favour of `str(model)`, devtools is a much better approach.

This is a bigger than I had hoped for during v1 betas, however users have done something seriously wrong if they're parsing the output of `str(x)` or `repr(x)` and I think this is much better than what went before.

This can't be merged until either all docs examples changed, or we setup an automatic way of generating the print output in examples (I'm going to work on this).

In #5052 we validated it by creating a ton of generics and measuring memory usage, not by checking the size of the cache. I'm a bit surprised by your tests behavior but not _too_ surprised, I don't know if it's easy to measure these things at this fine of a level.

I did a sanity check:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete

del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

assert len(cache) == 0  # actually 1
```

So it seems this would not work in the first place!

Ok I think I found the issue:

```python
import gc
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
from weakref import WeakValueDictionary

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyGeneric(Generic[T]):
    pass

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

Concrete = MyGeneric[int]
cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete
del Concrete

gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

referrer = next(iter(gc.get_referrers(next(cache.values()))))
print(referrer)  # <functools._lru_cache_wrapper object at 0x102dee560>
print(referrer.__module__)  # typing
```

So it looks like this cache inside of `_tp_cache` of `typing.py` may be holding onto a reference.
It has a `maxsize` of 128, which basically means that the `WeakValueDict` will act as a regular dict for the _last_ 128 things that got run through it!

That explains why the test that creates thousands of objects and measures memory consumption looks like it's not accumulating but this one measuring just 1 reference does.

cache: WeakValueDictionary[Any, Any] = WeakValueDictionary()

    cache[(MyGeneric, int)] = Concrete
    del Concrete

create_and_del()
gc.collect(0)
gc.collect(1)
gc.collect(2)

for r in gc.get_referrers(next(cache.values())):
    print(r, end="\n\n")
```

If you find this crazy _early and _late cache key business hard to understand, I can explain in more detail (probably makes sense to add comments to these functions but wanted to see if you ended up wanting to simplify it first).

This approach was necessary to get `Model[List[T]][int]` to be the same type as `Model[List[int]]`. It could be modified to not use two different cache keys at different points, but the `_early_cache_key` is optimized to be as quick to compute as possible (for repeated-access speed), and the `_late_cache_key` is optimized to be as "correct" as possible, so that two types that are ultimately the same after resolving the type arguments will always produce cache hits.

If we only wanted one (or two in the case of single-item-inputs to `__class_getitem__`) cache keys per type, we would either need to always use the slower/more computationally intensive logic associated with `_late_cache_key`, or would need to accept that `Model[List[T]][int]` is a different type than `Model[List[T]][int]`. I'm hesitant to accept this last point given that currently, an instance of type `Model[List[T]][int]` will fail validation for a field of type `Model[List[int]]`. That said, I think we may need to change that behavior anyway.

I did some digging into what was going on with the calls to get_args in the v1 cache key logic, and as far as I could tell the only thing it was really doing for us was helping us differentiate between the ordering of items in Unions (e.g., `Union[int, float]` vs. `Union[float, int]`). (It's definitely possible I'm missing other cases where it's relevant.)

I have pulled out this function to do exactly this check, and more "correctly" by applying to each item in a possible tuple (which is not currently done in v1), and ignoring the args for other types (besides Union) where order is not ignored and therefore not important (and differences in the result of get_args for other origin types can cause spurious cache misses).

context.commit_message:
Refactor and optimize schema cleaning logic (#11244)

The existing `_WalkCoreSchema` logic is replaced by a new schema cleaning logic. While the existing logic was traversing the core schemas multiple times to:
- collect schemas with references (replacing them with `'definition-reference'` schemas)
- counting the number of definition references
- replace `'definition-reference'` by its definition, if possible
- figure out schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied
- collect invalid schemas

We know apply a single *read-only* pass on the core schemas to:
- collect all definition references, so that we can drop unused definitions
- collect `'definition-reference'` if it appears only once, and then mutate it *in place* to be the definition it points to.
- collect schemas that need to have discriminated unions applied

The two biggest changes here are:
- the schema traversing is read-only, there's not initial copy of it like we used to do in the first `_WalkCoreSchema` pass. Because we mutate `'definition-reference'` schemas in place, this could lead to other model schemas mutated. In practice, this shouldn't happen.
- Referenceable schemas are not transformed into `'definition-reference'` schemas first. If a schema is fetched from a `__pydantic_core_schema__` property, and this schema contains a referenceable schema that is also present in the root schema, they won't be collected as a single definition.

The extra step to collect invalid schemas was also removed, although this could be added back without any performance degradation.

The schema traversing code is implemented in Python. Doing so in Rust provides a small performance improvement, but having it defined in Python provides easier maintenance. This might get revisited in the future.

Thanks @MarkusSintonen for looking into this first and designing the new schema traversing logic.

Co-authored-by: Markus Sintonen <markus.sintonen@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: sydney-runkle <sydneymarierunkle@gmail.com>

context.pr_body:
I would recommend reviewing this commit by commit, though looking over the whole thing afterwards gives some helpful perspective as well.

Changes in this PR:
* Remove the `CoreMetadataHandler` structure - it offered minimal type checking benefits, some overhead, and a good amount of unnecessary complexity.
* Better documentation for the `CoreMetadata` dict so that it's clear what we're adding to it and why.
* Remove as much of the json schema (callable) generation logic from `_generate_schema.py` and `_known_annotated_metadata.py` and consolidate it in `json_schema.py`
* For basic json schema updates and `json_schema_extra` updates, no longer build a callable ahead of time.
* As a nice benefit, seeing some 2-5% improvements in schema build times, which is good considering this is just JSON schema related changes.

TODOs, in the future:
* Minimize amount of callable wrapper logic we need for JSON schema generation - requires a major refactor, unfortunately.
* Move the `CoreMetadata` structure to rust so that we can pull out some of the `cast` calls and just get natural type checking benefits there. One hiccup here is that replacing `metadata: dict[str, Any]` with `metadata: CoreMetadata`, doesn't allow for arbitrary injection (say, in a custom schema), so I'm not sure what we want to do about that. It also then raises errors when we do our temporary injects for say, discriminator application, but we shouldn't be doing that anyway.
* Standardize whether or not we simplify refs for callable json schema application so we don't need `pydantic_js_functions` and `pydantic_js_annotation_functions`

I'd love @PrettyWood @hramezani @tiangolo @adriangb and others to review this. Having to fix some suggestions, but given how big this is, I might defer some suggestions to subsequent PRs.

I'm sorry there's so much noise - obviously it would be great if the interesting bits could be in a different PR to the refactoring, but that wasn't possible while keeping tests "passing".

Test situation now:
* 1367 passed
* 92 skipped
* 732 xfailed - marked as allowed to fail to keep CI passing
* 210 xpassed - in files marked as allowed to fail, but passing

There's a lot still to do, but the core functionality is now working using pydantic-core.

## Summary of changes

* internal logic has been move (mostly) into the `_internal` module - this is to provide a clear differentiating between the public API and internal functions
* Type constraints (like `constr`, `UUID5` `FilePath`) having been converted to type annotations, although some have an alias to simplicity
* Most of the logic to generate pydantic-core schema from python types is done
* test modules that are mostly failing (or make no sense at the moment) have been marked as xfail, as features are fixed, we can remove the xfails and fix the tests
* mypy, pyright and linting are passing ~~(though the mypy tests are currently xfail), fixed~~
* docs examples are not run at the moment, re-building docs is probably the biggest thing to do
* model methods like `dict()` have not yet been renamed, we'll do that on a future PR

Before merging we need to decide on https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/307.

---

In terms of next steps, I'm going to create issues now rather than listing here.

Using the `|` operator for type unions will not work in Python versions below 3.10.

It works fine as long as you have `from __future__ import annotations` so annotations are ignored at runtime.

Hence why tests are passing on 3.7, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11.

Oh, I wasn't aware of that. Thank you for the clarification.

My apologies for not verifying that it does indeed work in the lower versions of Python.
no problem, I agree it's odd - it's a new innovation for me to use new type hints in code targeted at old versions by using `from __future__ import annotations`.

@skip_not_37
def test_forward_ref_sub_types(create_module):
    module = create_module(
        """
from typing import ForwardRef, Union

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Leaf(BaseModel):
    a: str


TreeType = Union[ForwardRef('Node'), Leaf]


class Node(BaseModel):
    value: int
    left: TreeType
    right: TreeType


Node.update_forward_refs()
    """
    )
    Node = module.Node
    Leaf = module.Leaf
    data = {'value': 3, 'left': {'a': 'foo'}, 'right': {'value': 5, 'left': {'a': 'bar'}, 'right': {'a': 'buzz'}}}

    node = Node(**data)
    assert isinstance(node.left, Leaf)
    assert isinstance(node.right, Node)

The Feature is talked in the issue. https://github.com/samuelcolvin/pydantic/issues/463

- _ForwardRef
